# POS-BIAS-MEASURE: Position Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge for Pairwise Comparison — A Measurement Study with Defined Metrics, Falsifiable Hypotheses, and Statistical Analysis Plan

**Authors:** PaperAI Automated Research Protocol  
**Affiliations:** Open-Source Automated Science Initiative  
**Manuscript Type:** Registered Report / Measurement Study (Literature Survey Mode)  
**Protocol Version:** v1.0 (2025-07-14)  
**Status:** Pre-Registration — Experiments Not Executed  

---

## Abstract

**Context and Motivation.** Large Language Models (LLMs) have become the de facto standard for automated evaluation of generative outputs via the *LLM-as-a-Judge* paradigm, with pairwise comparison serving as the dominant protocol in leaderboards, reward modeling, and model selection. The validity of this paradigm is threatened by *position bias*—the systematic tendency of a judge to prefer an answer based on its presentation order rather than its intrinsic quality. Despite widespread acknowledgment of this threat, the literature lacks a unified measurement framework: prior studies operationalize position bias heterogeneously (repetition stability, position consistency, preference fairness, raw agreement flip rate, composite cognitive bias scores), rarely control for answer-quality gaps or prompt-length asymmetry, and predominantly report point estimates without confidence intervals, statistical tests, or minimum sample-size justifications.

**Objectives.** This study establishes a measurement framework for position bias in pairwise LLM judging, contributing: (1) two precisely defined, computable metrics—Swap Rate (SR) and First-Position Preference Rate (FPR)—with mathematical definitions and estimators; (2) two falsifiable hypotheses (H1, H2) with explicit equivalence bounds for falsification ($\delta_{\text{SR}} = 0.02$, $\delta_{\text{FPR}} = 0.01$); (3) a complete pre-registered statistical analysis plan comprising exact binomial hypothesis tests, bootstrap percentile confidence intervals ($B = 10{,}000$), and an analytical minimum sample-size derivation (Wilson score, conservative $p=0.5$) yielding $N_{\min} = 4{,}802$ pairs; (4) an experimental protocol using public human-annotated pairwise datasets (LLMBar-Natural, MT-Bench Human Judgments), 2–3 judge models spanning parameter scales (7B, 70B, API), bidirectional evaluation of each pair, and $R \ge 3$ independent runs; (5) a systematic mapping of prior operationalizations against the proposed metrics.

**Methods.** For a set of $N$ pairwise instances $(q, a_1, a_2, y)$, each judge $J$ evaluates both presentation orders $\pi \in \{(1,2), (2,1)\}$. SR quantifies decision inconsistency under swap: $\text{SR} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{1}[d_i^{(1,2)} \neq d_i^{(2,1)}]$. FPR quantifies directional preference for the first position: $\text{FPR} = \frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^N (\mathbb{1}[d_i^{(1,2)}=1] + \mathbb{1}[d_i^{(2,1)}=2])$. H1 (SR > 0) is tested via one-sided exact binomial test against $\delta_{\text{SR}}$; H2 (FPR $\neq$ 0.5) via two-sided exact binomial test. Uncertainty is quantified via percentile bootstrap per run and bootstrap-of-means across runs. Quality-gap stratification (tertiles of human preference margin) probes bias–gap interaction.

**Results.** Not Exp. (experiments not yet executed per Registered Report protocol).

**Conclusions.** This work does not propose a new judging method or debiasing technique. It contributes a measurement and analysis protocol that clarifies what prior studies measured, specifies the incremental measurement contribution, and provides a reproducible statistical framework for quantifying position bias in pairwise LLM evaluation. All design parameters (sample size, API calls, computational budget) are derivable from declared values.

**Keywords:** LLM-as-a-Judge, pairwise comparison, position bias, swap rate, first-position preference rate, falsifiable hypothesis, bootstrap confidence interval, minimum sample size, registered report

---

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 Motivation and Background

The adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) as automated evaluators—termed *LLM-as-a-Judge*—has fundamentally reshaped the evaluation landscape for generative AI [14, 2, 11]. Among the protocols employed, pairwise comparison has emerged as the dominant paradigm: given a prompt $q$ and two candidate answers $a_1, a_2$, the judge $J$ selects the preferred answer. This protocol underpins major leaderboards (e.g., Chatbot Arena [2]), reward modeling pipelines for alignment [15], and model selection workflows [11]. The appeal is clear: pairwise judgments align well with human preference, scale efficiently, and avoid the calibration challenges of absolute scoring.

However, the epistemic validity of pairwise LLM judgments is threatened by a systematic phenomenon known as *position bias*: the tendency of the judge to favor an answer based on its position in the input context (first vs. second) rather than its semantic quality [8, 5, 16]. Unlike human evaluators, who can be instructed to ignore order or counterbalanced via experimental design, LLM judges process the concatenated prompt $P(q, a_{\pi(1)}, a_{\pi(2)})$ as a single sequence. The autoregressive nature of Transformer decoders, combined with attention mechanisms that may weight early tokens differently [10], creates a structural pathway for position-dependent preferences. If unmeasured and uncorrected, position bias injects systematic error into leaderboard rankings, reward model training signals, and downstream model selection decisions.

The urgency of rigorous measurement is amplified by the expanding scope of LLM-as-a-Judge deployments. High-stakes decisions—model release gating, benchmark leaderboard rankings, reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) reward signals—now hinge on pairwise judgments. A bias magnitude of even a few percentage points can flip pairwise outcomes in closely matched comparisons, distorting the very signals these systems are designed to capture. Yet, as we detail in Section 1.2, the current literature lacks the measurement rigor required to quantify this threat with statistical guarantees.

### 1.2 Limitations of Existing Baselines

Despite growing recognition of position bias [1, 4, 8, 5, 16, 9, 13, 10], the literature exhibits four structural limitations that undermine cumulative scientific progress.

**Heterogeneous Operational Definitions.** Prior studies operationalize "position bias" under at least five distinct metrics, preventing direct comparison or meta-analysis. Shi et al. [8] introduce three metrics—*repetition stability* (agreement on repeated same-order prompts), *position consistency* (agreement between $(A,B)$ and $(B,A)$ decisions), and *preference fairness* (balance of wins when positions swapped)—but do not isolate a single primary metric with a standard estimator. Norman et al. [5] report a "raw agreement flip rate" exceeding 0.10 for two of 21 judges, yet do not define the estimator formally nor distinguish swap inconsistency from directional preference. Soumik [16] states "position bias $\le 0.04$" without specifying the exact metric, rendering the claim unfalsifiable. Koo et al. [9, 13] measure a composite *COBBLER* score aggregating six cognitive biases, which does not isolate position bias in the pairwise setting. Çelik [10] studies primacy/recency effects in single-essay scoring—a related but distinct task where the judge scores one output at a time rather than comparing two. This fragmentation means that a statement such as "Judge X exhibits position bias of 0.08" is semantically ambiguous without a shared definition.

**Insufficient Control for Confounders.** Position bias is confounded by the quality gap between answers and by prompt-length asymmetry. Shi et al. [8] observe that position consistency degrades sharply when answer quality is similar (low $\Delta$) and that prompt-length imbalance exacerbates bias. Yet, few studies stratify by quality gap or equalize prompt length. Without stratification, an overall bias estimate conflates two regimes: ambiguous pairs where bias may dominate, and clear-quality-gap pairs where the correct answer may overcome positional influence. This conflation obscures the conditions under which bias is practically consequential.

**Absence of Inferential Statistics.** The majority of studies report point estimates without confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or power analyses [8, 5, 16]. Norman et al. [5] conduct 118 runs across 21 judges but report no confidence intervals for position bias estimates. Without uncertainty quantification, one cannot distinguish a true bias of 0.02 from a sampling fluctuation of 0.02. Without pre-specified hypothesis tests and equivalence bounds, claims of "negligible bias" or "severe bias" are rhetorical rather than statistical. The lack of minimum sample-size derivations further implies that study sizes are driven by convenience rather than statistical precision targets.

**No Pre-Registered Falsifiable Hypotheses.** Existing work is exploratory; no study states primary hypotheses with explicit falsification conditions prior to data collection. In a measurement science context, this permits *post hoc* selection of metrics, thresholds, and subsets that support a desired narrative. A rigorous measurement study must declare: what is measured (metric definitions), what constitutes evidence for/against the phenomenon (hypotheses with equivalence bounds), and what sample size ensures adequate precision (power/precision analysis)—all before observing data.

Table 1 summarizes the measurement landscape, contrasting prior operationalizations with the framework proposed herein.

**Table 1: Prior Position Bias Operationalizations vs. POS-BIAS-MEASURE Metrics**

| Prior Operationalization | Source | Metric Name(s) | Key Difference from POS-BIAS-MEASURE |
|--------------------------|--------|----------------|--------------------------------------|
| Repetition Stability | Shi et al. [8] | Fraction of identical decisions on repeated same-order prompts | Measures self-consistency, not position-swap effect |
| Position Consistency | Shi et al. [8] | Agreement between $(A,B)$ and $(B,A)$ decisions | Equivalent to $1 - \text{SR}$ but not named/isolated as primary metric; no CI |
| Preference Fairness | Shi et al. [8] | Balance of wins when positions swapped | Related to FPR but defined only for balanced subsets |
| Raw Agreement Flip Rate | Norman et al. [5] | Proportion of pairs where judgment flips on swap | Same as SR but reported as point estimate only; no falsification bounds |
| COBBLER Aggregate Bias | Koo et al. [9, 13] | Composite cognitive bias score (6 biases) | Not specific to position bias in pairwise setting |
| Primacy/Recency in Essay Scoring | Çelik [10] | Section-weight shift in single-essay scoring | Different task (scoring vs pairwise comparison) |
| Unspecified "Position Bias $\le 0.04$" | Soumik [16] | Not explicitly defined | Metric ambiguity; our work defines SR/FPR explicitly |

### 1.3 Core Contributions

This study **does not** propose a new judging architecture, prompting strategy, or debiasing method. It contributes a *measurement protocol*—a set of definitions, hypotheses, statistical procedures, and experimental designs—that can be adopted by any researcher or platform evaluating LLMs via pairwise comparison. The five core contributions are:

- **C1. Unified Metric Definitions.** We provide precise mathematical definitions of Swap Rate (SR) and First-Position Preference Rate (FPR) with their estimators (Section 3.2). SR captures *inconsistency under swap* (does the decision change when positions are exchanged?), while FPR captures *directional preference for the first position* (does the judge favor whoever is presented first?). This distinction resolves the ambiguity in prior work where "position bias" conflates instability with directional preference.

- **C2. Falsifiable Hypotheses with Equivalence Bounds.** We pre-register two hypotheses with explicit falsification conditions (Section 3.3):
  - **H1 (Existence of Swap Bias):** $\text{SR} > 0$. Falsified if the upper bound of the 95% CI for SR $\le \delta_{\text{SR}} = 0.02$.
  - **H2 (Directional First-Position Bias):** $\text{FPR} \neq 0.5$. Falsified if the 95% CI for FPR is entirely contained in $[0.5 - \delta_{\text{FPR}}, 0.5 + \delta_{\text{FPR}}]$ with $\delta_{\text{FPR}} = 0.01$.
  These bounds represent practically negligible effect sizes: $\delta_{\text{SR}} = 0.02$ corresponds to 1 decision flip per 50 pairs; $\delta_{\text{FPR}} = 0.01$ corresponds to a 1% deviation from chance, well below the $>0.10$ flip rates reported by Norman et al. [5].

- **C3. Complete Statistical Analysis Plan.** We specify (Section 3.4): (a) exact binomial hypothesis tests (one-sided for H1 against $\delta_{\text{SR}}$, two-sided for H2 against 0.5); (b) bootstrap percentile confidence intervals ($B = 10{,}000$ resamples) per run, with bootstrap-of-means for cross-run aggregation; (c) analytical minimum sample-size derivation using the Wilson score interval under conservative variance ($p=0.5$), yielding $N_{\min,\text{SR}} = 2{,}401$ pairs for target half-width $h_{\text{SR}} = 0.02$ and $N_{\min,\text{FPR}} = 4{,}802$ pairs for $h_{\text{FPR}} = 0.01$; (d) quality-gap stratification protocol (tertiles of human preference margin) with Cochran–Armitage trend test for monotonicity.

- **C4. Experimental Protocol with Variance Control.** We declare a fully specified protocol (Section 3.5): public human-annotated pairwise datasets (LLMBar-Natural, MT-Bench Human Judgments, HH-RLHF subset) with $N \ge 5{,}000$ pairs; 2–3 judge models spanning parameter scales (7B, 70B, frontier API); bidirectional evaluation (both orders per pair); $R = 3$ independent runs with temperature $T=0$ for determinism; full computational budget accounting (API calls, GPU-hours, token estimates). All design parameters are derivable from the declared values in the Global Notation Lock Table.

- **C5. Systematic Mapping of Prior Measurements.** Table 1 and the analysis in Section 5.2 trace each prior study's operationalization to the POS-BIAS-MEASURE metrics, clarifying exactly what is new (unified definitions, CIs, falsification bounds, sample-size derivation, stratification) versus what replicates or extends prior measurements.

### 1.4 Paper Organization

The remainder of this manuscript is organized as follows. **Section 2** (Related Work) provides an expanded categorization of prior work on LLM-as-a-Judge biases, cognitive biases in LLM evaluation, and statistical methods for pairwise comparison measurement. **Section 3** (Methodology) formalizes the problem setting, defines SR and FPR with estimators, states the falsifiable hypotheses and equivalence bounds, details the statistical analysis plan (hypothesis tests, bootstrap CIs, minimum sample-size derivation, quality-gap stratification), specifies the experimental protocol (datasets, judges, prompts, runs, computational budget), and presents a process diagram of the evaluation pipeline. **Section 4** (Experiments) presents the experimental design summary table and the results table templates (Tables 2–4) with all values marked "Not Exp." per Registered Report requirements, alongside the computational budget breakdown. **Section 5** (Discussion) outlines the interpretation framework for hypothesis outcomes, compares the proposed measurements to prior operationalizations, and discusses practical implications for leaderboard operators and model developers. **Section 6** (Limitations) enumerates six scope and generalizability limitations. **Section 7** (Threats to Validity) details five validity threats (construct, internal, external, statistical conclusion, measurement) with pre-registered mitigations. **Section 8** lists the locked reference anchors. **Appendix A** provides the full minimum sample-size calculation details. **Appendix B** provides the bootstrap procedure pseudocode.

## 2. Related Work

### 2.1 Multi-Dimensional Taxonomy of Paradigms

We structure the landscape of LLM-as-a-Judge bias research along six dimensions critical for measurement rigor: **evaluation setting** (pairwise, list-wise, scoring), **bias taxonomy scope** (position-specific vs. general cognitive), **metric formalization** (named metric, estimator, confidence interval), **confounder control** (quality gap, length, style), **statistical rigor** (hypothesis test, power analysis, multi-run variance), and **debiasing focus** (measurement vs. mitigation). Table 1 contrasts prior operationalizations against these dimensions.

**Table 1: Taxonomy and Comparative Overview of Existing Paradigms in LLM-as-a-Judge Bias Measurement**

| Study | Setting | Bias Taxonomy Scope | Metric Formalization (Name, Estimator, CI) | Confounder Control | Statistical Rigor (Test, Power, Multi-run) | Primary Focus |
|-------|---------|---------------------|--------------------------------------------|-------------------|-------------------------------------------|---------------|
| Jeong et al. [1,4] | Pairwise vs. Pointwise | Position bias (qualitative claim) | None (qualitative: "biases exacerbated") | No | No test, no power, no multi-run | Conceptual analysis |
| Shi et al. [8] | Pairwise & List-wise | Position bias (3 sub-metrics) | Repetition Stability, Position Consistency, Preference Fairness (point estimates only) | Weak (length); Quality gap noted as major confounder | No CI, no power analysis, single run per config | Systematic measurement |
| Norman et al. [5] | Pairwise (single rubric) | Position bias (flip rate), Consistency, Agreement | Raw Agreement Flip Rate (>0.10) (point estimate) | No | 118 runs for reliability; no CI for bias magnitude, no power | Large-scale reliability audit |
| Koo et al. [9,13] | Preference Ranking | 6 Cognitive Biases (COBBLER) | Composite COBBLER Score (aggregate, no position-specific estimator) | No | Statistical significance tests; no power analysis for position bias | Cognitive bias benchmark |

| Gu et al. [14] | Survey (Taxonomy) | Taxonomy of biases (Position, Verbosity, etc.) | None (survey) | N/A | N/A | Literature synthesis |

**Key Observations from Taxonomy.**
- **Metric Ambiguity**: No prior work defines a *Swap Rate* (SR) with a precise estimator $\widehat{\text{SR}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum \mathbb{1}[d^{(1,2)} \neq d^{(2,1)}]$ and a *First-Position Preference Rate* (FPR) with estimator $\widehat{\text{FPR}} = \frac{1}{2N}\sum (\mathbb{1}[d^{(1,2)}=1] + \mathbb{1}[d^{(2,1)}=2])$ as primary, distinct metrics. Shi et al. [8]’s "Position Consistency" equals $1 - \text{SR}$ but is not isolated as a primary estimand with CI. Norman et al. [5]’s "Flip Rate" aligns with SR but lacks directional decomposition (FPR). Soumik [16] reports a scalar "Position Bias ≤ 0.04" without defining the underlying random variable.
- **Confounder Neglect**: Quality-gap stratification—critical because bias magnitude is theoretically conditional on $\Delta$ (human preference margin)—is absent in [1,4,5,9,13,16]. Shi et al. [8] acknowledge quality gap as a dominant factor but do not stratify estimates.
- **Inferential Vacuum**: With the exception of Çelik [10] (different task) and Norman et al. [5] (reliability, not bias magnitude), no study reports confidence intervals for position bias estimates, conducts hypothesis tests with pre-specified equivalence bounds, or derives minimum sample size $n_{\min}$ analytically. Multi-run variance decomposition (within-run vs. between-run) is not standard practice.

### 2.2 Deep Comparative Analysis of Existing Mechanisms

#### 2.2.1 Position-Bias-Specific Measurement Studies

**Shi et al. [8] (Judging the Judges)** provides the most comprehensive measurement to date. They operationalize three metrics on 15 judges across MT-Bench and DevBench: (1) *Repetition Stability*: agreement on repeated same-order prompts; (2) *Position Consistency*: agreement between $(A, B)$ and $(B, A)$ orders; (3) *Preference Fairness*: win-rate balance when positions are swapped. While Position Consistency is mathematically equivalent to $1 - \text{SR}$, the authors do not treat SR as a population parameter requiring estimation with uncertainty quantification. The study identifies quality gap as a primary moderator ("bias is stronger when quality gap is small") but reports only aggregate point estimates. No confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or sample-size justifications are provided. The experimental design uses a single run per judge-configuration, conflating sampling variance with potential API non-determinism.

**Norman et al. [5] (Reliability without Validity)** conduct a massive-scale audit (541k judgments, 21 judges). They report a "Raw Agreement Flip Rate" exceeding 0.10 for two proprietary judges, confirming position bias prevalence. However, the metric is reported as a global point estimate per judge. The 118 runs are used to estimate *reliability* (inter-run agreement), not to construct CIs for the bias metric itself. The study does not control for quality gap, prompt length asymmetry, or directional preference (FPR). The conclusion "reliability without validity" underscores the need for the falsifiable hypotheses (H1, H2) and equivalence bounds ($\delta_{\text{SR}}, \delta_{\text{FPR}}$) proposed in this work.

**Soumik [16] (Bias Mitigation Strategies)** evaluates nine debiasing techniques (e.g., swap augmentation, rubric calibration). The paper reports "Position Bias ≤ 0.04" for the best configuration but does not explicitly define the random variable measured. The evaluation uses subsets of MT-Bench (400), LLMBar (200), and a custom set (375), totaling < 1,000 pairs—below the $n_{\min,\text{FPR}} = 4,802$ derived in §3.4.3 for a target half-width $h_{\text{FPR}} = 0.01$. Statistical correction (Holm-Bonferroni) is applied across mitigation strategies, but no power analysis or CI for the bias metric itself is reported. This highlights the distinction between *mitigation benchmarking* (which requires a measurement standard) and *measurement protocol design* (this work’s contribution).

**Jeong et al. [1,4] (The Comparative Trap)** argue theoretically and empirically that pairwise comparison amplifies biases inherent in pointwise scoring. Their measurement of position bias is qualitative ("biases are exacerbated"), serving as a motivation for rigorous quantification rather than a measurement protocol itself.

#### 2.2.2 General Cognitive Bias Benchmarks

**Koo et al. [9,13] (COBBLER)** introduce a benchmark for six cognitive biases (egocentrism, order effect, etc.) in LLM evaluators. "Order Effect" in COBBLER corresponds to position bias but is measured as a component of a composite score across diverse tasks (summarization, dialogue, etc.). The metric is an aggregate accuracy drop or preference shift, not a pairwise swap-rate estimator. The benchmark is valuable for broad bias profiling but lacks the granularity to isolate SR and FPR in a controlled pairwise setting with quality-gap stratification. Our work complements COBBLER by providing the specific measurement instrument for the "Order Effect" dimension in pairwise comparison.

#### 2.2.3 Adjacent Task: Automated Essay Scoring

**Çelik [10]** investigates primacy/recency effects in *single-essay scoring* (not pairwise comparison). The study uses linear mixed models to detect section-weight shifts (intro vs. body vs. conclusion) across 192 synthetic essays. While statistically rigorous (reporting p-values, effect sizes), the task structure differs fundamentally: the judge scores one essay at a time, and "position" refers to textual segment order, not answer presentation order in a pair. The statistical machinery (mixed models, CI for coefficients) demonstrates the feasibility of inferential statistics in LLM evaluation, which we adapt to the pairwise setting via exact binomial tests and bootstrap CIs for proportions.

#### 2.2.4 Surveys and Taxonomies

**Gu et al. [14] (Survey on LLM-as-a-Judge)** provides a taxonomy categorizing biases into *Position Bias*, *Verbosity Bias*, *Self-Enhancement Bias*, etc. It synthesizes existing metrics but does not propose new definitions or resolve the ambiguities identified in Table 1. It confirms the community's need for a unified measurement standard.

### 2.3 Theoretical & Practical Gaps in Current Literature

Synthesizing the taxonomy and mechanistic analysis, we identify five specific gaps that the POS-BIAS-MEASURE framework (Section 3) addresses. These gaps map directly to the locked contributions C1–C5 in the Blueprint.

**Gap 1: Absence of Unified, Distinct Metric Definitions with Estimators (→ C1).**
Prior work conflates *inconsistency* (does the decision flip?) with *directionality* (does the judge prefer the first slot?). Shi et al. [8]’s Position Consistency captures inconsistency; Preference Fairness captures directionality but only on a balanced subset. Norman et al. [5]’s Flip Rate captures inconsistency. No study defines both SR (inconsistency) and FPR (directionality) as population parameters with explicit estimators ($\widehat{\text{SR}}, \widehat{\text{FPR}}$) and a clear mathematical relationship (SR = 0 ⇒ FPR = 0.5 under no directional bias). This conflation prevents diagnosing *why* a judge is biased (random flipping vs. systematic first-slot preference).

**Gap 2: Lack of Falsifiable Hypotheses with Equivalence Bounds (→ C2).**
Existing studies are exploratory: they report point estimates (e.g., "Flip Rate > 0.10" [5], "Bias ≤ 0.04" [16]) without a pre-registered decision rule. The concept of "practically negligible bias" is absent. We introduce equivalence bounds $\delta_{\text{SR}} = 0.02$ and $\delta_{\text{FPR}} = 0.01$ derived from leaderboard reporting granularity (1 swap per 50 pairs, 1% deviation from chance) and the magnitude of bias reported in [5] (>0.10). The falsification conditions—CI containment in equivalence region—provide a binary, reproducible decision criterion missing in [1,4,5,8,16].

**Gap 3: Missing Statistical Analysis Plan with Analytical Power Justification (→ C3).**
No prior work derives minimum sample size $n_{\min}$ from a target CI half-width $h$ for a proportion estimator. Shi et al. [8] use ~3,000 pairs (MT-Bench) without justification. Norman et al. [5] use 541k judgments for reliability, not bias precision. Soumik [16] uses < 1,000 pairs. We derive $n_{\min,\text{SR}} = 2,401$ and $n_{\min,\text{FPR}} = 4,802$ pairs using the conservative Wilson score approximation ($p=0.5, z=1.96$) for target half-widths $h_{\text{SR}}=0.02, h_{\text{FPR}}=0.01$. We further specify the exact inferential pipeline: exact binomial tests (H1 vs $\delta_{\text{SR}}$, H2 vs 0.5), percentile bootstrap (B=10,000) for per-run CIs, and bootstrap-of-means for cross-run aggregation.

**Gap 4: No Variance Decomposition Protocol (→ C4).**
API-based judges exhibit non-determinism even at temperature $T=0$ [5]. Local models may have hardware-induced variance. Prior work either runs once [8,16] or aggregates 118 runs for reliability without decomposing variance sources [5]. We mandate $R \ge 3$ independent runs and require reporting: (a) per-run point estimates, (b) within-run bootstrap variance (sampling uncertainty), (c) between-run variance (systematic non-determinism), enabling the variance decomposition in Table 4 (Blueprint).

**Gap 5: Unsystematic Mapping of Prior Measurements (→ C5).**
Because metrics are heterogeneously defined and unnamed, it is difficult to ascertain what exactly a new study replicates or extends. Table 1 (Blueprint §4) and Table 1 (this section) provide a traceable mapping: each prior operationalization is linked to its metric name, estimator (if any), and difference from SR/FPR. This clarifies that POS-BIAS-MEASURE does not "re-invent" measurement but *standardizes* and *formalizes* the swap-rate and directional-preference constructs latent in [5,8,16].

---

**Summary.** The literature converges on the *existence* of position bias but diverges on *what* is measured, *how precisely*, and *with what statistical guarantee*. The POS-BIAS-MEASURE framework proposed in Section 3 does not introduce a new debiasing technique; it introduces a **measurement protocol**—definitions (C1), falsification logic (C2), analysis plan (C3), experimental design (C4), and literature mapping (C5)—to transform position bias from a qualitative concern into a quantifiable, auditable property of LLM judges.

## 3. Proposed Methodology

Phần này trình bày khung đo lường **POS-BIAS-MEASURE** bao gồm: hình thức hóa bài toán toán học (§3.1), đường ống kiến trúc tổng thể (§3.2), định nghĩa chi tiết các thành phần đo lường và thống kê (§3.3), giao thức thực thi thuật toán (§3.4), và phân tích lý thuyết về độ phức tạp (§3.5). ### 3.1 Formal Problem Formulation & Mathematical Foundations

Chúng ta xem xét bài toán đánh giá cặp (pairwise evaluation) trong bối cảnh LLM-as-a-Judge. Không gian mẫu và các biến ngẫu nhiên được định nghĩa chính xác như sau.

**Không gian đầu vào (Input Space).** Một thể hiện so sánh cặp là một bộ tứ $ (q, a_1, a_2, y) $ trong đó:
- $ q \in \mathcal{Q} $: câu hỏi/hướng dẫn (prompt) đầu vào.
- $ a_1, a_2 \in \mathcal{A} $: hai câu trả lời ứng viên.
- $ y \in \{1, 2\} $: nhãn ưu tiên của người (ground-truth human preference), $ y=1 $ nghĩa là $ a_1 $ tốt hơn $ a_2 $.

**Thứ tự trình bày (Presentation Order).** Một hoán vị $ \pi \in \Pi = \{(1,2), (2,1)\} $ quyết định thứ tự xuất hiện của $ a_1, a_2 $ trong prompt đưa cho giám khảo. Prompt có thứ tự được ký hiệu là $ P(q, a_{\pi(1)}, a_{\pi(2)}) $.

**Mô hình giám khảo (Judge Model).** $ J $ là một hàm xác định (deterministic function) ánh xạ từ chuỗi prompt đến quyết định nhị phân:

$$
J: \text{String} \to \{1, 2\}
$$

Chúng ta cố định nhiệt độ $ T = 0 $ để đảm bảo tính xác định tối đa; bất kỳ phi xác định nào từ API (ví dụ: race condition) được xử lý qua nhiều lần chạy độc lập $ R \ge 3 $.

**Quyết định quan sát (Observed Decisions).** Với thể hiện thứ $ i $ ($ i = 1, \dots, N $), ký hiệu $ d_i^{(\pi)} = J(P(q_i, a_{i,\pi(1)}, a_{i,\pi(2)})) $ là quyết định của giám khảo dưới thứ tự $ \pi $. Cặp quyết định quan sát được cho thể hiện $ i $ là $ (d_i^{(1,2)}, d_i^{(2,1)}) $.

**Mục tiêu đo lường.** Ước lượng hai tham số dân số:
1.  **Tỷ lệ đổi phán quyết (Swap Rate - SR):** Xác suất phán quyết thay đổi khi hoán đổi vị trí.
2.  **Tỷ lệ ưu tiên vị trí đầu (First-Position Preference Rate - FPR):** Xác suất giám khảo chọn câu trả lời ở vị trí đầu bất kể nội dung.

Hai tham số này tách biệt *tính không nhất quán do vị trí* (SR) khỏi *xu hướng định hướng* (FPR).

### 3.3 Detailed Component Formulations

Phần này định nghĩa chính xác các ước lượng điểm, khoảng tin cậy, giả thuyết thống kê, và cỡ mẫu tối thiểu.

#### 3.3.1 Metric Definitions & Estimators

Theo **Định nghĩa 1 (Swap Rate - SR)** và **Định nghĩa 2 (First-Position Preference Rate - FPR)** trong Blueprint, chúng ta có các ước lượng điểm (estimators) cho một lần chạy đơn lẻ $ r $:

**Swap Rate Estimator:**

$$
\widehat{\text{SR}}^{(r)} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{1}\left[ d_{i}^{(1,2)} \neq d_{i}^{(2,1)} \right]
$$

trong đó $ \mathbb{1}[\cdot] $ là hàm chỉ báo (indicator function), $ d_{i}^{(\pi)} $ là quyết định của cặp $ i $ tại lần chạy $ r $ (chỉ số $ r $ bị ẩn để gọn).

**First-Position Preference Rate Estimator:**

$$
\widehat{\text{FPR}}^{(r)} = \frac{1}{2N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left( \mathbb{1}\left[ d_{i}^{(1,2)} = 1 \right] + \mathbb{1}\left[ d_{i}^{(2,1)} = 2 \right] \right)
$$

Lưu ý: Mẫu quan sát cho FPR có kích thước $ 2N $ (mỗi cặp đóng góp 2 quan sát "vị trí đầu").

**Mối quan hệ toán học.** Nếu $ \text{SR} = 0 $ (hoàn toàn nhất quán), thì $ \text{FPR} = 0.5 $ ngụ ý không có thiên lệch định hướng. Nếu $ \text{SR} > 0 $, FPR đo lường xu hướng *ròng* (net preference) cho vị trí đầu.

#### 3.3.2 Falsifiable Hypotheses with Equivalence Bounds

Chúng ta thiết lập hai giả thuyết thống kê có điều kiện bác bỏ (falsification conditions) rõ ràng dựa trên **khoảng tương đương (equivalence bounds)** $ \delta_{\text{SR}} = 0.02 $ và $ \delta_{\text{FPR}} = 0.01 $.

| Hypothesis | Null Hypothesis ($ H_0 $) | Alternative ($ H_1 $) | Falsification Condition (Reject $ H_1 $ / Accept $ H_0 $) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **H1** (Existence) | $ \text{SR} \le \delta_{\text{SR}} $ | $ \text{SR} > \delta_{\text{SR}} $ | Upper bound of 95% CI for SR $ \le \delta_{\text{SR}} $ |
| **H2** (Directionality) | $ |\text{FPR} - 0.5| \le \delta_{\text{FPR}} $ | $ |\text{FPR} - 0.5| > \delta_{\text{FPR}} $ | 95% CI for FPR $ \subset [0.5 - \delta_{\text{FPR}}, 0.5 + \delta_{\text{FPR}}] $ |

*Cơ sở lý luận cho bounds:* $ \delta_{\text{SR}} = 0.02 $ tương đương 1 lần đổi phán quyết trên 50 cặp, thấp hơn ngưỡng báo cáo điển hình trong leaderboard. $ \delta_{\text{FPR}} = 0.01 $ tương ứng độ lệch 1% so với ngẫu nhiên, nhỏ hơn đáng kể ngưỡng $ >0.10 $ báo cáo bởi Norman et al. [5].

#### 3.3.3 Statistical Inference Procedures

**A. Kiểm định giả thuyết chính xác (Exact Binomial Tests).**

- **H1 Test:** Kiểm định nhị thức chính xác một phía. Thống kê kiểm định: $ K = N \cdot \widehat{\text{SR}} $. Giá trị $ p $: $ p = \mathbb{P}(X \ge K \mid n=N, p=\delta_{\text{SR}}) $.
- **H2 Test:** Kiểm định nhị thức chính xác hai phía. Số lần thử $ n = 2N $. Số thành công $ K = \sum_{i=1}^N (\mathbb{1}[d_i^{(1,2)}=1] + \mathbb{1}[d_i^{(2,1)}=2]) $. Giá trị $ p $: $ p = 2 \cdot \min(\mathbb{P}(X \le K), \mathbb{P}(X \ge K)) $ dưới $ \text{Binomial}(2N, 0.5) $.

**B. Bootstrap Percentile Confidence Intervals (B = 10,000).**

Đối với mỗi lần chạy $ r $, chúng ta thực hiện lấy mẫu bootstrap cấp cặp (pair-level resampling) để bảo toàn cấu trúc phụ thuộc giữa hai thứ tự của cùng một cặp.

1.  Tạo $ B $ mẫu bootstrap $ \mathcal{D}^{*(b)} $ ($ b=1..B $) bằng cách lấy mẫu có hoàn lại $ N $ chỉ số từ $ \{1..N\} $.
2.  Tính $ \widehat{\text{SR}}^{*(b)}, \widehat{\text{FPR}}^{*(b)} $ trên mỗi mẫu.
3.  Khoảng tin cậy percentile 95%: $ \text{CI}_{0.95} = [Q_{0.025}, Q_{0.975}] $ của phân phối bootstrap.

**C. Tổng hợp qua các lần chạy (Cross-Run Aggregation).**

Điểm ước lượng cuối cùng: $ \overline{\text{SR}} = \frac{1}{R} \sum_{r=1}^R \widehat{\text{SR}}^{(r)} $, $ \text{Std}_{\text{SR}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{R-1}\sum_{r=1}^R (\widehat{\text{SR}}^{(r)} - \overline{\text{SR}})^2 } $.
Khoảng tin cậy của giá trị trung bình: Bootstrap-of-means (lấy mẫu có hoàn lại từ $ \{\widehat{\text{SR}}^{(1)}, \dots, \widehat{\text{SR}}^{(R)}\} $, $ B=10,000 $).

#### 3.3.4 Minimum Sample Size Derivation (Analytical)

Chúng ta dẫn xuất cỡ mẫu $ N $ tối thiểu để đảm bảo bán kính khoảng tin cậy (half-width) $ h $ cho ước lượng Wilson score không vượt quá ngưỡng mục tiêu.

Công thức bán kính Wilson score cho tỷ lệ $ p $, cỡ mẫu $ n $, mức ý nghĩa $ \alpha $ ($ z = z_{\alpha/2} $):

$$
h(n, p, z) = \frac{z}{1 + z^2/n} \sqrt{ \frac{p(1-p)}{n} + \frac{z^2}{4n^2} }
$$

Sử dụng xấp xỉ bảo thủ $ p = 0.5 $ (phương sai cực đại) và $ n \gg z^2 $, ta có công thức mẫu số đơn giản:

$$
n_{\min} \approx \left\lceil \frac{z^2 \cdot 0.25}{h^2} \right\rceil
$$

**Đối với SR ($ h_{\text{SR}} = 0.02 $):**

$$
n_{\min, \text{SR}} = \left\lceil \frac{1.96^2 \times 0.25}{0.02^2} \right\rceil = \left\lceil 2401 \right\rceil = 2{,}401 \text{ pairs}
$$

**Đối với FPR ($ h_{\text{FPR}} = 0.01 $, số quan sát $ n = 2N $):**

$$
n_{\min, \text{FPR}} = \left\lceil \frac{1.96^2 \times 0.25}{0.01^2} \right\rceil = 9{,}604 \text{ observations} \implies N_{\min} = 4{,}802 \text{ pairs}
$$

**Quyết định thiết kế:** Chọn $ N = 5{,}000 $ cặp (vượt cả hai ranh giới). Nếu tập dữ liệu công khai có $ < 5{,}000 $ cặp, sử dụng toàn bộ và báo cáo bán kính CI thực tế đạt được (achieved precision).

#### 3.3.5 Quality-Gap Stratification Protocol

Để kiểm soát biến gây nhiễu "chênh lệch chất lượng" (quality gap $ \Delta $), chúng ta phân tầng tập dữ liệu:
1.  Tính margin ưu tiên người $ \Delta_i $ cho mỗi cặp $ i $ (nếu tập dữ liệu có điểm số lượng; nếu chỉ có nhãn nhị phân, dùng độ đồng thuận của nhiều annotator hoặc gán $ \Delta=1 $ cho cặp adversarial, $ \Delta=0.5 $ cho cặp close).
2.  Chia thành 3 tertiles (Stratum 1: Low $ \Delta $, Stratum 2: Medium, Stratum 3: High).
3.  Báo cáo $ \widehat{\text{SR}}_k, \widehat{\text{FPR}}_k $ cho mỗi stratum $ k \in \{1,2,3\} $.
4.  Kiểm định xu hướng đơn điệu (Cochran-Armitage trend test) để kiểm tra xem thiên lệch có giảm khi $ \Delta $ tăng không (giả thuyết của Shi et al. [8]).

### 3.4 Algorithmic Execution Protocol

Thuật toán 1 quy trình hóa toàn bộ quy trình từ nạp dữ liệu đến báo cáo kết quả, đảm bảo tính tái lập (reproducibility).

**Algorithm 1: POS-BIAS-MEASURE Evaluation Protocol**

```python
# Algorithm 1: POS-BIAS-MEASURE Evaluation Protocol
# Input: 
#   D = {(q_i, a1_i, a2_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^N  # Dataset of N pairs
#   Judges = {J_1, ..., J_J}                # J judge models (e.g., 7B, 70B, API)
#   R = 3                                   # Number of independent runs
#   B = 10000                               # Bootstrap resamples
#   alpha = 0.05                            # Significance level
#   delta_SR = 0.02, delta_FPR = 0.01       # Equivalence bounds
#   PromptTemplate(q, a_A, a_B) -> str      # Fixed prompt function
# Output: 
#   Results dict with SR, FPR, CIs, p-values, falsification flags per judge

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import binomtest

def compute_metrics(d1, d2):
    """d1, d2: arrays of shape (N,) with values in {1, 2}"""
    N = len(d1)
    sr = np.mean(d1 != d2)
    fpr = (np.sum(d1 == 1) + np.sum(d2 == 2)) / (2 * N)
    return sr, fpr

def bootstrap_ci(d1, d2, B=10000, alpha=0.05):
    N = len(d1)
    boot_sr, boot_fpr = [], []
    for _ in range(B):
        idx = np.random.choice(N, N, replace=True)
        sr_b, fpr_b = compute_metrics(d1[idx], d2[idx])
        boot_sr.append(sr_b)
        boot_fpr.append(fpr_b)
    ci_sr = np.percentile(boot_sr, [100*alpha/2, 100*(1-alpha/2)])
    ci_fpr = np.percentile(boot_fpr, [100*alpha/2, 100*(1-alpha/2)])
    return ci_sr, ci_fpr

def exact_binom_test_h1(sr_hat, N, delta=0.02):
    # H0: SR <= delta vs H1: SR > delta
    k = int(round(sr_hat * N))
    # Use binomtest with alternative='greater', null proportion = delta
    res = binomtest(k, N, p=delta, alternative='greater')
    return res.pvalue

def exact_binom_test_h2(fpr_hat, N):
    # H0: FPR = 0.5 vs H1: FPR != 0.5
    # Total trials = 2N, successes = fpr_hat * 2N
    k = int(round(fpr_hat * 2 * N))
    res = binomtest(k, 2*N, p=0.5, alternative='two-sided')
    return res.pvalue

def run_protocol(D, Judges, R, B, alpha, delta_SR, delta_FPR):
    results = {}
    N = len(D)
    
    for J_name, J_model in Judges.items():
        run_srs, run_fprs = [], []
        run_decisions = [] # Store for bootstrap-of-means
        
        for r in range(R):
            # Set seed for reproducibility (affects API non-determinism, data shuffle)
            np.random.seed(r * 1000 + hash(J_name) % 1000)
            
            d_order12 = np.zeros(N, dtype=int)
            d_order21 = np.zeros(N, dtype=int)
            
            # Evaluate all pairs in both orders
            for i, (q, a1, a2, y) in enumerate(D):
                # Order (1,2): a1 is A, a2 is B
                prompt12 = PromptTemplate(q, a1, a2)
                d_order12[i] = J_model.generate(prompt12, temperature=0)
                
                # Order (2,1): a2 is A, a1 is B
                prompt21 = PromptTemplate(q, a2, a1)
                d_order21[i] = J_model.generate(prompt21, temperature=0)
            
            # Compute metrics for this run
            sr, fpr = compute_metrics(d_order12, d_order21)
            run_srs.append(sr)
            run_fprs.append(fpr)
            run_decisions.append((d_order12.copy(), d_order21.copy()))
            
            # Per-run Bootstrap CI
            ci_sr, ci_fpr = bootstrap_ci(d_order12, d_order21, B, alpha)
            # Store per-run CI if needed
        
        # Aggregate across runs
        mean_sr, std_sr = np.mean(run_srs), np.std(run_srs, ddof=1)
        mean_fpr, std_fpr = np.mean(run_fprs), np.std(run_fprs, ddof=1)
        
        # Bootstrap-of-means CI for the mean
        boot_means_sr, boot_means_fpr = [], []
        for _ in range(B):
            idx = np.random.choice(R, R, replace=True)
            boot_means_sr.append(np.mean([run_srs[i] for i in idx]))
            boot_means_fpr.append(np.mean([run_fprs[i] for i in idx]))
        ci_mean_sr = np.percentile(boot_means_sr, [100*alpha/2, 100*(1-alpha/2)])
        ci_mean_fpr = np.percentile(boot_means_fpr, [100*alpha/2, 100*(1-alpha/2)])
        
        # Hypothesis Tests on Mean Estimates
        p_h1 = exact_binom_test_h1(mean_sr, N, delta_SR)
        p_h2 = exact_binom_test_h2(mean_fpr, N)
        
        # Falsification Check (CI containment)
        # H1 falsified if Upper CI <= delta_SR
        h1_falsified = ci_mean_sr[1] <= delta_SR
        # H2 falsified if CI inside [0.5 - delta_FPR, 0.5 + delta_FPR]
        h2_falsified = (ci_mean_fpr[0] >= 0.5 - delta_FPR) and (ci_mean_fpr[1] <= 0.5 + delta_FPR)
        
        results[J_name] = {
            "SR": (mean_sr, std_sr, ci_mean_sr),
            "FPR": (mean_fpr, std_fpr, ci_mean_fpr),
            "p_H1": p_h1, "p_H2": p_h2,
            "H1_falsified": h1_falsified, "H2_falsified": h2_falsified,
            "per_run": {"SR": run_srs, "FPR": run_fprs}
        }
        
        # Stratified Analysis (if quality gap Delta available)
        # ... (omitted for brevity, follows same pattern per stratum)
        
    return results
```

**Chú thích Thuật toán 1:**
- Hàm `PromptTemplate` được cố định cho tất cả giám khảo để loại bỏ biến thiên prompt.
- `temperature=0` ép buộc giải mã tham lam (greedy decoding); seed numpy kiểm soát thứ tự duyệt dữ liệu và phi xác định API tiềm ẩn.
- `binomtest` từ `scipy.stats` triển khai kiểm định Clopper-Pearson chính xác (exact binomial test).

### 3.5 Theoretical Analysis & Asymptotic Complexity

Phần này phân tích độ phức tạp tính toán và bộ nhớ của giao thức, cùng các bảo đảm thống kê tiệm cận.

#### 3.5.1 Computational Complexity

Gọi $ N $ là số cặp, $ J $ số mô hình giám khảo, $ R $ số lần chạy, $ B $ số mẫu bootstrap, $ L $ độ dài trung bình token của prompt + câu trả lời.

**Độ phức tạp thời gian (Time Complexity):**
1.  **Inference (Chủ đạo):** Mỗi cặp yêu cầu 2 lần gọi mô hình (forward pass). Tổng số forward passes: $ 2 \times N \times J \times R $.
    - Với mô hình cục bộ (local): $ \mathcal{O}(N \cdot J \cdot R \cdot L \cdot C_{\text{model}}) $, trong đó $ C_{\text{model}} $ là chi phí FLOPs/token (tỷ lệ với số tham số).
    - Với API: Chi phí thời gian chủ yếu là độ trễ mạng (latency), song song hóa được qua batch request.
2.  **Bootstrap (Phụ):** $ \mathcal{O}(J \cdot R \cdot B \cdot N) $ cho việc tính toán chỉ số trên mảng NumPy (rất nhanh, $ \ll 1 $ giây cho $ B=10^4, N=5\times10^3 $).
3.  **Tổng cộng:** $ \mathcal{O}(N \cdot J \cdot R \cdot (L \cdot C_{\text{model}} + B)) $. Với $ N=5000, J=3, R=3, B=10^4 $: Phần inference chiếm $ >99.9\% $ thời gian.

**Độ phức tạp không gian (Space Complexity):**
- Lưu trữ quyết định: $ \mathcal{O}(J \cdot R \cdot N) $ integers (2 bytes/int $ \approx 5000 \times 3 \times 3 \times 2 \approx 90 $ KB).
- Bootstrap samples: Không lưu trữ toàn bộ mẫu (streaming), chỉ lưu phân phối thống kê $ \mathcal{O}(B) $ floats ($ \approx 80 $ KB).
- **Tổng bộ nhớ RAM:** $ \mathcal{O}(N + B) $, hoàn toàn phù hợp môi trường CPU đơn giản (không cần GPU cho phần phân tích).

**Ngân sách tính toán dẫn xuất (Derivable Budget):**
| Component | Formula | Value (N=5000, J=3, R=3) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Total Forward Passes | $ 2 N J R $ | 90,000 |
| API Tokens (est. 200 tok/call) | $ 2 N J R \times 200 $ | 18M tokens |
| API Cost (est. $0.15/M) | $ \text{Tokens} \times 0.15 / 10^6 $ | ~$2.70 |
| GPU Hours (7B, 0.5s/call) | $ 90,000 \times 0.5 / 3600 $ | ~12.5 hrs (single GPU) |
| GPU Hours (70B, 3s/call) | $ 90,000 \times 3 / 3600 $ | ~75 hrs (2xA100) |

*Lưu ý: Các con số trên dẫn xuất trực tiếp từ tham số đã khóa ($ N, J, R, B $) và ước lượng token/latency tiêu chuẩn, không chứa giả định ẩn.*

#### 3.5.2 Statistical Asymptotics & Guarantees

**Bổ đề 1 (Consistency of Estimators).** Với $ N \to \infty $, $ \widehat{\text{SR}} \overset{p}{\to} \text{SR} $ và $ \widehat{\text{FPR}} \overset{p}{\to} \text{FPR} $ theo Định luật lớn (LLN) vì chúng là trung bình mẫu của các biến ngẫu nhiên i.i.d. có giới hạn $ [0,1] $.

**Bổ đề 2 (Asymptotic Normality of Bootstrap CI).** Dưới điều kiện chuẩn (Donsker class), khoảng tin cậy percentile bootstrap $ [Q_{\alpha/2}, Q_{1-\alpha/2}] $ đạt độ phủ tiệm cận $ 1-\alpha $ cho cả SR và FPR. Với $ N=5000 $, xấp xỉ chuẩn là hợp lý; tuy nhiên chúng ta dùng percentile bootstrap (không giả định chuẩn) để an toàn cho mẫu hữu hạn.

**Bổ đề 3 (Type I Error Control for Falsification).** Quy tắc bác bỏ H1 dựa trên "Upper CI $ \le \delta_{\text{SR}} $" kiểm soát tỷ lệ lỗi loại I (falsely claiming no bias) ở mức $ \alpha $ khi $ \text{SR} = \delta_{\text{SR}} $, giả định độ phủ CI chính xác. Tương tự cho H2 với vùng tương đương $ [0.5-\delta_{\text{FPR}}, 0.5+\delta_{\text{FPR}}] $.

**Hạn chế lý thuyết (Theoretical Limitations):**
- **Phụ thuộc giữa các cặp:** Giả định i.i.d. có thể vi phạm nếu tập dữ liệu chứa các câu hỏi trùng lặp (duplicate prompts) hoặc câu trả lời được sinh từ cùng một mô hình nguồn. Chúng ta báo cáo độ đa dạng của tập dữ liệu trong §4 để giảm thiểu.
- **Phi xác định API:** Kiểm định nhị thức chính xác giả định $ N $ quan sát độc lập. Phi xác định API tại $ T=0 $ vi phạm giả định này nhẹ. Việc báo cáo phương sai giữa các lần chạy (Between-run variance, Bảng 4) định lượng mức độ vi phạm này.
- **Nhãn người nhiễu:** Phân tầng theo $ \Delta $ giả định nhãn người là ground truth. Nhiễu nhãn làm giảm sức mạnh kiểm định xu hướng (attenuation bias) nhưng không làm sai lệch ước lượng SR/FPR tổng thể.

## 4. Experiments and Results

### 4.1 Benchmark Datasets, Metrics & Evaluation Protocol

Chúng tôi tuân thủ chính xác giao thức thực nghiệm đã đăng ký trong **Blueprint (§3.5, §3.1, §3.4)**. Phần này trình bày chi tiết các thành phần dữ liệu, chỉ số đo lường và quy trình đánh giá để đảm bảo tính tái lập hoàn toàn.

**Bộ dữ liệu benchmark (Benchmark Datasets).** Chúng tôi chọn ba tập dữ liệu so sánh cặp công khai, có nhãn ưu tiên người (human-annotated pairwise preference), đáp ứng tiêu chí kích thước $N \ge 5{,}000$ cặp và độ đồng thuận cao:

1.  **LLMBar-Natural** [8, 16]: Tập con tự nhiên (natural) của LLMBar, chứa $\approx 5{,}000+$ cặp hỏi-đáp đa lĩnh vực (general chat, coding, reasoning) với nhãn ưu tiên người đạt đồng thuận rõ ràng. Tập này được thiết kế để kiểm tra thiên lệch đối kháng (adversarial bias) nhưng tập con *Natural* phản ánh phân phối sử dụng thực tế.
2.  **MT-Bench Human Judgments** [2, 8]: Bộ nhãn so sánh cặp do người gán cho MT-Bench (multi-turn, coding, reasoning, extraction), khoảng $3{,}000+$ cặp. Dùng bổ sung để kiểm tra tính tổng quát hóa cross-domain.
3.  **HH-RLHF Pairwise Subset** [15]: Tập dữ liệu lớn ($\approx 50{,}000+$ cặp) từ quy trình RLHF (Helpful/Harmless). Chúng tôi lấy mẫu ngẫu nhiên $5{,}000$ cặp có độ đồng thuận cao (majority vote $\ge 2/3$ annotators) để đảm bảo nhãn gold-standard.

**Quy tắc chọn lọc (Selection Rule):** Theo Blueprint §3.1, ưu tiên tập dữ liệu lớn nhất có $\ge 5{,}000$ cặp với nhãn cặp rõ ràng. Nếu không đạt, sử dụng toàn bộ dữ liệu có sẵn và báo cáo độ rộng CI thực tế (achieved CI half-width).

**Chỉ số đánh giá (Evaluation Metrics).** Chúng tôi khóa chặt hai chỉ số chính (Primary Metrics) và ba nhóm chỉ số thứ cấp (Secondary/Exploratory Metrics) theo **Blueprint §3.2, §3.3**:

- **Chính (Primary):**
    - **Tỷ lệ đổi phán quyết (Swap Rate, SR):** $\widehat{\text{SR}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{1}[d_i^{(1,2)} \neq d_i^{(2,1)}]$. Đo lường sự không nhất quán khi hoán vị.
    - **Tỷ lệ ưu tiên vị trí đầu (First-Position Preference Rate, FPR):** $\widehat{\text{FPR}} = \frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^N \left(\mathbb{1}[d_i^{(1,2)}=1] + \mathbb{1}[d_i^{(2,1)}=2]\right)$. Đo lường xu hướng định vị (directional bias).

- **Thứ cấp / Khám phá (Secondary/Exploratory):**
    - **SR/FPR theo tầng chất lượng (Per-stratum SR/FPR):** $\widehat{\text{SR}}_k, \widehat{\text{FPR}}_k$ cho $k \in \{1,2,3\}$ (tertile của margin $\Delta$). Kiểm tra tương tác thiên lệch - khoảng cách chất lượng.
    - **Phân giải phương sai (Variance Decomposition):** Phương sai giữa các lần chạy (Between-run variance) và phương sai bootstrap trong lần chạy (Within-run bootstrap variance). Định lượng phi xác định API và biến động lấy mẫu.

**Giao thức đánh giá (Evaluation Protocol).** Mọi tham số tuân thủ **Blueprint §3.5, §3.4.2, §3.4.3**:

- **Mô hình giám khảo (Judge Models, $J=3$):**
    - *Judge-7B*: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (proxy cho 7B–8B scale).
    - *Judge-70B*: Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (proxy cho 70B–72B scale).
    - *Judge-API*: GPT-4o-mini (frontier API model, chi phí kiểm soát).
- **Tham số sinh (Generation Config):** Temperature $T = 0$ (deterministic), Top-p $= 1.0$, Max new tokens $= 10$ (chỉ sinh token 'A' hoặc 'B').
- **Template Prompt:** Cố định cho tất cả mô hình: `"Compare Answer A and Answer B for the given question. Output only 'A' or 'B'."` Thứ tự trình bày được hoán đổi hệ thống: Order (1,2) và Order (2,1).
- **Số lần chạy (Runs, $R=3$):** Ba lần chạy độc lập với seed khác nhau (42, 123, 456) để ước lượng phương sai giữa các lần chạy (between-run variance), bao gồm cả phi xác định tiềm ẩn của API ở $T=0$.
- **Bootstrap:** $B = 10{,}000$ lần lấy mẫu lại (resamples) trên cấp độ cặp (pair-level) cho mỗi lần chạy để xây dựng CI percentile 95%.
- **Tổng ngân sách tính toán (Computational Budget):** Dẫn xuất từ $N=5{,}000, R=3, J=3$:
    - Tổng số lời gọi mô hình: $2 \times N \times R \times J = 90{,}000$ calls.
    - Chi tiết: API ($\approx 30{,}000$ calls, $\sim 18$M tokens, $\sim \$2.70$), Local 7B ($\sim 4.2$ GPU-hours trên A100), Local 70B ($\sim 50$ GPU-hours trên 2$\times$A100).

### 4.5 Qualitative Case Studies & Error Analysis

Phần này trình bày khung phân tích định tính (Qualitative Analysis Framework) và các ví dụ minh họa (Illustrative Examples) được xây dựng dựa trên các mẫu lỗi điển hình quan sát được trong tài liệu [5, 8, 16]. **Lưu ý:** Các case study dưới đây là *minh họa cho quy trình phân tích* (analysis protocol illustration), không phải kết quả thực nghiệm đã chạy.

**Quy trình phân tích định tính (Qualitative Analysis Protocol):**
1.  **Lọc mẫu Swap:** Từ kết quả Judge-7B (Run 1), trích xuất tập $S = \{ i \mid d_i^{(1,2)} \neq d_i^{(2,1)} \}$.
2.  **Phân loại lỗi (Error Taxonomy):** Gán nhãn thủ công cho 50 cặp ngẫu nhiên từ $S$ theo 4 loại:
    - **Type A: Content-Ignorant Positional Heuristic.** Mô hình chọn vị trí đầu bất kể nội dung (dấu hiệu FPR cao).

    - **Type C: Style/Format Bias.** Ưu tiên định dạng (markdown, bullet points) ở vị trí đầu.

## 5. Discussion

### 5.1 In-Depth Technical Analysis & Trade-Offs

The POS-BIAS-MEASURE framework introduces a deliberate separation between *swap inconsistency* (SR) and *directional preference* (FPR). This distinction addresses a conflation present in prior operationalizations. Shi et al. [8] report "position consistency" (equivalent to $1 - \text{SR}$) and "preference fairness" (related to FPR but defined only on balanced subsets), while Norman et al. [5] report a raw flip rate without directional decomposition. By defining SR and FPR as population parameters with explicit estimators ($\widehat{\text{SR}}$, $\widehat{\text{FPR}}$), we enable a granular diagnosis: a judge may exhibit high SR (instability under permutation) while maintaining FPR $\approx 0.5$ (no net directional bias), or vice versa. This separation informs mitigation strategy selection—calibration-based methods target FPR, while consistency regularization targets SR.

**Trade-off: Metric Granularity vs. Statistical Power.**
Defining two primary metrics necessitates a multiple-comparison correction or a larger sample size to maintain family-wise error rate. Our analytical sample-size derivation (§3.4.3) is driven by the stricter requirement of FPR ($h_{\text{FPR}} = 0.01$), yielding $N_{\min} = 4,802$ pairs. This conservative bound ensures adequate power for both metrics simultaneously but increases computational cost. For the API judge (Judge-API), 30,000 calls ($2 \times N \times R \times 1$) incur non-trivial latency and monetary cost (~$0.90 at assumed rates). For local 70B inference, ~50 GPU-hours on 2×A100 represents a significant allocation. Researchers with constrained budgets may relax $h_{\text{FPR}}$ to 0.015 (reducing $N_{\min}$ to ~2,135 pairs) or reduce $R$ to 2 (sacrificing between-run variance estimation), but such deviations must be declared *a priori* to preserve the registered-report integrity.

**Trade-off: Determinism (Temperature = 0) vs. Ecological Validity.**
We fix temperature $T = 0$ to isolate position bias from sampling variance. However, production LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines often employ $T > 0$ (e.g., $T=0.7$ in Chatbot Arena [2]) to encourage diversity or break ties. At $T > 0$, the observed SR conflates *position-induced flips* with *stochastic flips*. Our protocol captures API non-determinism at $T=0$ via between-run variance (Table 4), but this underestimates total variance under stochastic decoding. A pragmatic extension is a nested design: $R_{\text{outer}}$ seeds for position order, $R_{\text{inner}}$ seeds for decoding stochasticity per order. This would increase calls by factor $R_{\text{inner}}$ but enable variance decomposition $\text{Var}(\text{SR}) = \text{Var}_{\text{position}} + \text{Var}_{\text{sampling}}$.

**Trade-off: Quality-Gap Stratification Granularity vs. Stratum Sample Size.**
Stratification by human preference margin $\Delta$ (tertiles) controls for the confounder identified by Shi et al. [8] (bias magnitude correlates with quality gap). However, splitting $N=5,000$ into three strata yields ~1,667 pairs per stratum. The per-stratum CI half-width for SR widens to $\approx 1.96 \times \sqrt{0.25 / 1667} \approx 0.024$, exceeding the target $h_{\text{SR}} = 0.02$. This is an accepted limitation: stratum estimates are exploratory (flagged as such in §3.4.4 and Table 3), and the primary inferential claim rests on the overall $N=5,000$ estimate. If a specific stratum is the target of inference (e.g., "bias in ambiguous pairs"), a dedicated study with $N_{\text{stratum}} \ge 2,401$ is required.

### 5.2 Threats to Validity & Honest Limitations

We explicitly acknowledge the following limitations, categorized by validity type, extending the pre-declared threats in Blueprint §10.

**Construct Validity.**
- **Metric Completeness:** SR and FPR capture *pairwise* position effects. They do not detect list-wise biases (e.g., "middle neglect" in $k>2$ comparisons) or context-dependent biases (e.g., bias magnitude changes with prompt length asymmetry). Çelik [10] observes primacy/recency shifts in single-essay scoring; our pairwise swap metric cannot capture such effects.
- **Prompt Template Sensitivity:** All metrics are conditional on the fixed prompt template (§3.5). Prior work [8, 16] shows bias magnitude varies with instruction phrasing, few-shot examples, and output format constraints (e.g., "Output only 'A' or 'B'" vs. "Explain your reasoning then output"). Our reported SR/FPR are *lower bounds* for the specific template; a template inducing stronger bias would yield higher estimates. We do not claim generalizability across prompt designs.
- **Human Label Noise:** Quality-gap stratification relies on human annotations $y$ as ground truth. Inter-annotator agreement on LLMBar-Natural [8, 16] is high but not perfect. Label noise attenuates the observed correlation between $\Delta$ and SR (regression dilution), potentially masking a true bias–gap interaction.

**Internal Validity.**
- **API Non-Determinism at $T=0$:** Closed-source APIs (GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-Haiku) may exhibit non-determinism even at temperature 0 due to batching, hardware non-determinism, or model updates. We mitigate by reporting between-run variance (Table 4) and using local models (7B, 70B) for fully deterministic baselines. However, if API non-determinism is systematic (e.g., correlated with position), it could inflate SR spuriously. We cannot fully rule this out without provider guarantees.
- **Model Version Drift:** For API judges, the model version may update between runs or during the study period. We mitigate by pinning model identifiers (e.g., `gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18`) and completing all runs within a short window, but version drift remains a threat for reproducibility.

**External Validity.**
- **Dataset Domain:** LLMBar-Natural and MT-Bench [2, 8] cover general chat, coding, and reasoning. They under-represent specialized domains (legal, medical, low-resource languages). Position bias may interact with domain-specific terminology or answer length distributions differently.
- **Judge Model Coverage:** Three models (7B, 70B, one API) span scale but not architecture (e.g., MoE vs. dense), alignment recipe (RLHF vs. DPO vs. constitutional AI), or quantization level (FP16 vs. 4-bit). Norman et al. [5] evaluate 21 judges; our $J=3$ is a minimal representative subset. Findings on scaling trends (7B vs. 70B vs. API) are indicative, not exhaustive.
- **Pairwise Protocol Only:** The study excludes pointwise scoring, list-wise ranking, and reference-guided evaluation. Jeong et al. [1, 4] argue pairwise amplifies bias relative to pointwise; our metrics quantify the pairwise case but do not test the amplification claim directly.

**Statistical Conclusion Validity.**
- **Multiple Comparisons:** Primary analysis comprises 6 tests (3 judges × 2 hypotheses). Strata add 18 exploratory tests (3 judges × 3 strata × 2 metrics). We report unadjusted $p$-values for strata with Bonferroni threshold noted ($\alpha/18 \approx 0.0028$). This increases Type II error for exploratory findings.
- **Equivalence Bound Arbitrariness:** $\delta_{\text{SR}} = 0.02$ and $\delta_{\text{FPR}} = 0.01$ are pragmatic choices (1 swap per 50 pairs; 1% deviation from chance). They are not derived from a formal cost-benefit analysis of downstream leaderboard errors. Different stakeholders (leaderboard operators vs. model developers) may require different bounds.

### 5.3 Emerging Frontiers & Open Research Directions

Based on the measurement gaps identified, we outline four open directions:

- **Direction 1: Distribution-Free Bias Certification for Leaderboards.**
  Current leaderboards (Chatbot Arena [2], MT-Bench) report Elo ratings without bias diagnostics. A practical frontier is a *bias certificate*: a periodic audit reporting SR/FPR with CIs for the active judge ensemble, coupled with a "bias-adjusted" rating that corrects for estimated FPR. This requires extending our pairwise protocol to the multi-model, multi-prompt, streaming setting of live arenas.

- **Direction 2: Causal Disentanglement of Position vs. Length vs. Style.**
  Position bias is confounded with answer length (first position often gets more tokens if template is asymmetric) and style (verbose vs. concise). A causal mediation analysis—intervening on length/style while holding position constant—would isolate the pure position effect. This requires synthetic counterfactual generation (e.g., length-controlled paraphrases) and structural causal modeling, moving beyond correlational stratification.

- **Direction 3: Adaptive Sequential Testing for Continuous Monitoring.**
  Our fixed-$N$ design is inefficient for continuous monitoring (e.g., nightly judge regression tests). Sequential probability ratio tests (SPRT) or anytime-valid confidence sequences [e.g., Waudby-Smith & Ramdas, 2024] would allow early stopping when SR is clearly $> \delta_{\text{SR}}$ or $< \delta_{\text{SR}}$, reducing average sample size by 30–50% while preserving Type I error. Integrating this into CI/CD pipelines for LLM evaluation is a high-impact engineering direction.

- **Direction 4: Position Bias in Multimodal and Tool-Use Judging.**
  As judges evaluate images, code execution traces, or tool-use trajectories (e.g., [11]), "position" generalizes to *presentation modality order* (image-first vs. text-first) or *tool-output order*. The swap-rate concept extends naturally: swap the presentation order of two multimodal candidates. Defining SR/FPR for these settings and measuring whether vision-language models exhibit stronger/weaker positional bias than text-only LLMs is an open empirical question.

---

## 6. Conclusion

This work presents POS-BIAS-MEASURE, a measurement and statistical analysis protocol for position bias in LLM-as-a-Judge pairwise comparison. We make five verifiable contributions: (C1) mathematically precise definitions of Swap Rate (SR) and First-Position Preference Rate (FPR) with computable estimators; (C2) two falsifiable hypotheses (H1: SR > 0, H2: FPR ≠ 0.5) with explicit equivalence bounds ($\delta_{\text{SR}} = 0.02$, $\delta_{\text{FPR}} = 0.01$) and binary falsification rules; (C3) a complete pre-registered statistical analysis plan including exact binomial tests, bootstrap percentile confidence intervals ($B=10,000$), and an analytical minimum sample-size derivation ($N_{\min} = 4,802$ pairs for $h_{\text{FPR}}=0.01$); (C4) an experimental protocol specifying public human-annotated datasets, bidirectional evaluation across 2–3 judge models of varying scale, $R \ge 3$ independent runs, and reporting standards (mean ± std, 95% CI); (C5) a systematic mapping (Table 1) contrasting prior operationalizations [1, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 13, 16] with our metrics, clarifying the incremental measurement contribution.

The study does not propose a new judging method, debiasing technique, or architectural modification. It provides a *ruler*—not a *hammer*. The experimental results (Tables 2–4) are marked "Not Exp." pending execution per the registered protocol. Upon execution, the binary falsification outcomes (H1 Falsified? / H2 Falsified?) will provide a clear, reproducible verdict on whether position bias is practically non-negligible for the tested judges under the specified conditions. We release the protocol, analysis code, and result templates to enable independent replication and extension to new judges, datasets, and prompt templates.
